subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]
passage: At six the hall in Ghent was full and the chief guest's chair was empty. Soo-ah, the stage manager, whispered, "The guest is stuck on the ring road." Tomas thought fast. The choir was scheduled after the speech, but they were already waiting in the wings. "Choir first," he said. "Then the guitar duo, then the speech when the guest arrives." Soo-ah rewrote the running order in ten seconds and told the presenter. The audience clapped through two songs, and when the guest slipped in at twenty to seven, the speech was next. Afterwards the team sat on the edge of the stage. "A twenty-minute buffer would have helped," said Soo-ah. Tomas wrote it on the checklist for next year.

qa.q: What was Tomas's first change to the running order?
qa.a: Tomas moved the choir first, before the guitar duo and the speech.

qa.q: How does Tomas seem to feel when the chief guest is late, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tomas seems calm under pressure, since he thinks fast and gives a clear new order without panic.

qa.q: What could the team add next year to avoid the problem, and why?
qa.a: They could build in a twenty-minute buffer near the start, because a delayed guest then does not force changes during the show.

qa.q: How might the audience have experienced the change?
qa.a: The audience probably noticed nothing wrong and enjoyed the music, since two songs began right away and the speech came when the guest arrived.

grounding: When the chief guest is late, the organiser moves the performance forward and adjusts the order, keeping the audience engaged, and the team later notes that a buffer would have helped.

passage:
At 10:40 the principal's secretary whispered to Trisha: "The chief guest is stuck in traffic. Maybe forty minutes."

Two hundred students sat in the school auditorium, already fidgeting. The programme said: lamp lighting, chief guest's speech, then the Class 10 dance.

Trisha looked at the running order and made up her mind. She ran backstage. "Rashmi, can your dancers go now?" Rashmi's eyes went wide, but she nodded. "Give me five minutes."

Trisha asked the anchor to announce a surprise. The dance went on first, then the quiz round, and the audience was clapping loudly by the time the guest walked in at 11:25. The lamp lighting and speech slid in after.

At the team meeting on Monday, Rashmi said, "We needed a spare fifteen minutes built in." Trisha wrote it on the planning sheet in capitals.

qa.q: What time did the chief guest walk in?
How did Rashmi feel when Trisha asked if the dancers could go now?
qa.a: Rashmi was startled and probably nervous, her eyes going wide, but she agreed willingly and asked for five minutes.

qa.q: What else could the team do next time besides adding a buffer?
qa.a: They could agree in advance on a backup order of items, so any organiser could switch it without having to decide under pressure.

qa.q: How did the change look to the students in the audience?
qa.a: For the students it probably felt like a lively surprise rather than a delay, so they stayed engaged instead of waiting restlessly.

grounding: Shows an organiser moving a performance forward when the chief guest is late, keeping the audience engaged, and the team later noting a buffer would have helped.

subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]
passage:
Dear Lavanya,

You'll laugh, but I finally understood what Miss Kurian meant about buffers.

Our Science Day assembly was supposed to open with a talk by a scientist from the university. At 9:00 she messaged: bus broke down, reaching by 9:45. I had 300 students on the ground and nothing planned for forty-five minutes.

My brain froze for about ten seconds. Then I grabbed the quiz team and asked them to start early. After the quiz I moved the model display forward and let kids walk around it. By the time the scientist arrived, people were still excited.

At our review, Aman said we should always keep fifteen spare minutes and one filler item ready. He's right. I'd been so proud of a tight timetable that I forgot tight means fragile.

Write soon,
Trisha

qa.q: How many students were on the ground?
qa.a: There were 300 students on the ground.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel in the first moments after the message?
qa.a: Trisha felt panicked and frozen for about ten seconds before recovering enough to act.

qa.q: What lesson does Trisha take from the review, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Trisha learns to keep fifteen spare minutes and a filler ready, because a timetable with no slack breaks as soon as one person is late.

qa.q: How might the waiting students have seen the morning?
qa.a: They probably saw a lively morning with a quiz and models, not a delay, so they stayed interested until the scientist came.

grounding: A letter shows an organiser reordering items when a guest is late to keep the audience engaged, then learning a buffer was needed.
